(The Frisky) -- There exists a school of thought that dictates if you think something catastrophic, then it won't happen. What would happen if my family died in a car accident? What would happen if my house caught on fire? "What makes men connect with the girl of their dreams after sparking with me?" the author asks. Two summers ago, I asked myself: Wouldn't it suck if my first love met someone unexpectedly and got over me before I could begin to move on? Thankfully, my family and my house are safe, but my feelings, my love life, and my ego still need mending. "I met someone." The text message appeared on the screen of my phone and I stopped walking. A group of my friends and I were leaving the movie theater, and it was as if all feelings he had for me were obliterated in one night. We broke up because he was studying in Europe. Poetically, we had expressed our feelings for each other just two nights before. Then he became someone else's boyfriend, and remained so, for much longer than he and I lasted. I should've known it would happen, since it happens quite often. My first kiss, who refused to be my boyfriend, met the girl of his dreams while I still ached for him. They're still together today. Since then, I've been the second choice for several more men. The most recent ones occurred this summer, when I tried and failed to win the heart of my friend Ken -- he started dating the person that he truly liked instead of settling for me. I lost Brian to his ex-girlfriend (although, in that case, I think they belonged together anyway). Each time, I laughed one of those sad, desperate guffaws -- here we go again! What makes men connect with the girl of their dreams after sparking with me? Another concept may be more applicable to my situation: the idea of a self-fulfilling prophecy. Perhaps I'm so aware of my "magic touch" that I'm making it happen. While the first love arrived in Europe, I even warned him what may happen. At the time, though, he waved the thought away. "I'm so picky, I rarely really like a girl like I like you," he typed. A month later, he must've been pleasantly shocked to discover my unfortunate power reached across the Atlantic Ocean. When Ken told me he was dating Mary, I was angry I'd let this happen to me again. I raged at him. He argued that it's irrational to use my past experience to predict the outcome of my future relationships (or my attempts at them). I'm sure that there'll be a guy someday who doesn't find me easy to move on from, but in the meantime I can't ignore the pattern and pretend that each time was a coincidence, as Ken had wanted me to do. I don't know if there is a way to avoid the seemingly inevitable. Each time I let my hopes conquer my superstition, there's a crash, a burn, a deflation, and the temporary loss of the ability to giggle, but I choose the chance of being the girl before the girlfriend over giving up the chance for breaking my streak. **The Stepping Stone Syndrome: Why Am I Always the Girl Before "The One"?**

*(The Frisky)* — There exists a psychological theory—or perhaps merely a form of superstitious coping—that imagining a disaster shields you from experiencing it. *What if my family died in a car crash? What if my house caught fire?* Two summers ago, I applied this logic to a more romantic brand of catastrophe, asking myself: *Wouldn't it be devastating if my first love unexpectedly met someone else and moved on before I even had the chance to?* 

Thankfully, my family and my home remain safe. My love life, heart, and ego, however, are still in desperate need of repair.

*"I met someone."* 

The words illuminated my phone screen, bringing me to a dead halt as I was leaving a movie theater with friends. In a single evening, it seemed every feeling he once harbored for me had vanished. Our breakup had been purely circumstantial—the result of his semester abroad in Europe—and, almost poetically, we had reaffirmed our deep affection for one another just two nights prior. Yet, practically overnight, he became someone else’s boyfriend, entering a relationship that ultimately far outlasted the brief time we spent together.

I should have anticipated it; after all, this script plays out in my life with alarming frequency. My first kiss—who refused to make our relationship official—met the girl of his dreams while I was still aching for him. They remain together to this day. In the years since, I have repeatedly found myself relegated to second choice. 

This past summer brought two fresh reminders. First, my failed attempt to win the heart of my friend Ken, who chose to pursue Mary—the person he truly desired—rather than settle for me. Then came Brian, whom I lost to his ex-girlfriend (though, to be fair, I believe they genuinely belonged together anyway). Each time, I could only manage a hollow, desperate laugh: *Here we go again.*

What is it about sparking a connection with me that seemingly prepares men to find the love of their lives? 

It raises a troubling question: am I experiencing a series of unfortunate coincidences, or am I orchestrating a self-fulfilling prophecy? Perhaps my hyper-awareness of this uncanny "magic touch" inadvertently manifests it. Before my first love departed for Europe, I even forewarned him of this tendency. He brushed my concern aside at the time, texting: *"I'm so picky, I rarely like a girl the way I like you."* Merely a month later, he must have been astonished to realize that my unfortunate spell possessed a transatlantic reach.

When Ken told me he was dating Mary, my frustration boiled over—not just at the situation, but at myself for allowing it to happen again. During our heated exchange, he argued that it was irrational to use past heartbreaks to predict the outcome of future romantic endeavors. While I logically trust that I will one day meet a man who does not find me so easily replaceable, I cannot simply dismiss these recurring outcomes as mere coincidences, as Ken urged me to do. 

I am unsure how to break this seemingly inevitable cycle. Every time my optimism overcomes my superstition, the resulting crash is painful, leaving me momentarily drained of all joy. Yet, I would still rather risk being the stepping stone to someone else's happily-ever-after than forfeit the chance of finally breaking my streak.

**Title:** The Catalyst: On Self-Fulfilling Prophecies and the Romance of the Placeholder

There is a distinct, agonizing grief in watching a man who swore he was unready for commitment propose to someone else six months after leaving your life. For years, this was the central, repeating motif of my romantic narrative. I wasn’t the woman men married; I was the woman they dated right before they met the woman they married. I was the layover, the trial run, the emotional crucible through which they passed only to emerge fully prepared to give another woman everything I had begged for. For a long time, I attributed this to a sort of cosmic bad luck, viewing myself as a romantic catalyst—a real-life "Good Luck Chuck." But a closer examination through the lens of psychological concepts reveals a far more uncomfortable truth: I was not cursed by the universe; I was trapped in a cage of my own design.

At the root of my romantic history lies the destructive habit of catastrophic thinking. Catastrophizing is a cognitive distortion wherein the mind automatically jumps to the worst possible outcome in any given situation. In the context of a budding relationship, where vulnerability is required, my brain perceived intimacy not as a source of connection, but as a threat. The moment a relationship began to feel meaningful, my anxiety would ignite. Instead of enjoying the quiet buildup of affection, I was hyper-fixated on the inevitable end. I mentally drafted breakup speeches while sitting across from men at dinner; I analyzed subtle shifts in their tone as definitive proof that their feelings were fading. In my mind, rejection was not a possibility—it was an absolute guarantee waiting to be realized.

This perpetual state of anticipation gave birth to a powerful self-fulfilling prophecy. A self-fulfilling prophecy occurs when a belief or expectation, whether true or false, brings about the very result it predicted. Driven by the fear of being blind-sided, I developed a habit of launching preemptive strikes. I began issuing warnings to the men I dated. "I’m just a phase for you," I would say with a light, self-deprecating laugh. Or, "You’re going to realize you want someone entirely different, and you’ll leave." 

I believed I was protecting myself by managing my expectations and laying my insecurities on the table. In reality, I was writing the script for my own abandonment. 

By constantly reminding these men of my perceived temporary status, I inadvertently gave them permission to treat me as such. I primed them to view our relationship not as a permanent destination, but as a temporary resting stop. My hyper-vigilance manifested as emotional distance, clinginess, and a pervasive, suffocating tension that drained the joy from our interactions. I became hard to love because I was constantly testing whether they would leave. Eventually, worn down by the emotional labor of constantly reassuring me—or simply subconsciously accepting the narrative I had repeatedly fed them—they left. 

And when they did, they carried with them the emotional maturity and self-awareness they had gained during our time together. I had conditioned them to seek clarity, stability, and ease—qualities my anxiety had rendered impossible in our dynamic. Unburdened by the weight of my catastrophic expectations, they walked straight into the arms of their next partners, ready to offer the deep, enduring love I had convinced them they couldn't share with me.

Recognizing this pattern is both painful and liberating. To realize that I have been a placeholder in my own love life because I cast myself in that role is a heavy burden to bear. Yet, it also means the curse is broken. I was never a stepping stone by nature; I was a victim of my own defense mechanisms. The cycle of heartbreaks was not an inescapable fate, but a loop powered by my own fears. Moving forward, breaking the cycle means learning to sit in the quiet vulnerability of love without bracing for the blow—refusing to write the end of the story before it has even had the chance to begin.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a personal essay about what it feels like to always be the "girl before the girlfriend"—the person guys date right before meeting the love of their lives.
counterfactuals.output:
There is a specific kind of magic I seem to possess, though it is not the sort they write fairy tales about. It is quieter, more practical, and infinitely more heartbreaking. I am the catalyst. The layover. The warm-up act before the main event. 

If you look at the romantic histories of the men I’ve loved, you’ll find a remarkably consistent trendline. I am the girl they date right before they meet the woman they marry.

It usually goes like this: I meet a man who is a work in progress. He is guarded, perhaps a little rough around the edges, emotionally clumsy, or adamant that he "isn't looking for anything serious right now." I fall for his potential. I bring my full, soft, patient self to the table. I teach him how to talk about his feelings instead of shutting down. I convince him that vulnerability isn't a weakness. I help him pick out better shirts, nudge him to fix his relationship with his sister, and listen to him process his deep-seated fears at two in the morning. 

We stay together for a year, maybe two. And then, inevitably, the relationship fray at the edges. He tells me he’s just not ready, or that he needs to "find himself," or that he loves me, but he’s not *in love* with me. Heartbroken, I gather my things and step aside.

Then comes the magic trick. 

Six months later—sometimes less—I scroll through Instagram and see him. He is standing on a beach, or in a sunlit kitchen, or in front of a Christmas tree. His arm is draped around a glowing girl. But it’s not just that he’s with someone new; it’s *how* he is with her. 

The man who "didn't believe in labels" has her name in his bio. The man who couldn't plan a date three days in advance has booked a trip to Tuscany. The man who was terrified of commitment is down on one knee with a diamond ring, less than a year after their first date. 

He didn't need time to "find himself." He just needed to find her. And he was able to love her so effortlessly because I spent two years teaching him how to hold the weight of another person's heart without dropping it.

To be the "girl before the girlfriend" is to exist in a strange, emotional purgatory. It leaves you feeling like a soft-launching pad for another woman's happily-ever-after. You become an unpaid consultant in the art of loving, doing all the heavy lifting, the emotional labor, and the remodeling, only for someone else to move into the finished house.

When it happens once, you call it bad timing. When it happens twice, you call it a coincidence. But when it becomes a pattern, it turns inward, mutating into a sharp, persistent question: *What is wrong with me?*

Why am I good enough to inspire growth, but not good enough to enjoy the harvest? Am I just a pit stop on the highway to someone else's soulmate? 

For a long time, I let this pattern erode my self-worth. I began to view myself as a museum of potential—a place men visited to learn something about themselves before moving on to the real world. I watched these men give their new partners the grand gestures, the unyielding loyalty, and the enthusiastic commitment I had begged for. It is a unique kind of humiliation to realize that a man was entirely capable of giving you what you needed; he just didn't think you were worth the effort.

But recently, the dust has begun to settle on my bitterness, leaving behind something clearer. 

I’ve started to realize that being the catalyst isn't a reflection of my inadequacy; it’s a reflection of my intensity. I love deeply, fiercely, and without reservation. I hold up a mirror to the people I date, asking them to meet me at a depth they have often never experienced before. Some men take that emotional maturity, learn from it, and realize they *do* want a real relationship—they just lack the courage to build it with the person who forced them to grow up. I was the mirror, but they wanted a fresh slate.

I’m learning to stop being the construction crew for men who are content to live in rubble until someone forces them to rebuild. I am realizing that my empathy, my capacity for intimacy, and my patience are not resources to be mined by men who are just passing through.

I don't want to be the dress rehearsal anymore. I don't want to be the lesson, or the stepping stone, or the bittersweet memory of the girl who taught them how to be a good partner. 

I want to be the destination. 

The next time a man tells me he isn't ready, I won't stick around to help him pack. I will leave him where he is, saving the magic of my love not for someone who needs to be taught how to hold it, but for someone who has been waiting his whole life for it to arrive.

# The “Good Luck Chuck” Complex: What Happens When You Become Modern Dating’s Human Layover?

There is a specific, ambient terror reserved for Sunday morning Instagram scrolling. You’re three sips into a latte, still wearing yesterday’s oversized t-shirt, when you see it: a hard-launch ring post from a guy you were sleeping with eighteen months ago. 

He looks happy. She looks glowing. And you feel like a ghost who just watched someone else move into the house you helped build.

Lately, I’ve been wrestling with a deeply unsettling theory: I am not a girlfriend; I am a romantic portal. I am the high-concept, indie-movie plot point that exists solely to prepare men for the love of their lives. 

If this sounds dramatic, let me present the evidence. 

Ex-boyfriend number one—let’s call him Leo—was the moody, poet-type who spent our entire nine-month relationship agonizing over whether he was "ready for something real." He moved to Madrid for a semester abroad, carrying a suitcase full of my tearful reassurance that he was worthy of a big, expansive life. Within three weeks of landing in Spain, he met a local photographer. They’ve been together for four years. Apparently, he *was* ready for something real; he just wasn’t ready for it with me. 

Then there was Ken. Ken was a long-time friend with whom I had an agonizing, two-year, "will-they-won't-they" dynamic that finally tipped into a late-night, messy hookup. For months, I tiptoed around his commitment phobia, playing the cool, low-maintenance girl who understood his "trauma around labels." A month after we finally fizzled out, Ken met a girl at a dog park. Within ninety days, they had moved in together. He now posts glowing paragraphs on her birthday. When we were together, I couldn't even get him to post a picture of my elbow.

After a while, the pattern stops feeling like a string of bad luck and starts feeling like a cosmic joke. You become a human stepping stone. You do the emotional heavy lifting—you teach them how to express their feelings, how to apologize, how to buy decent bedsheets—and then another woman reaps the benefits of your labor. You are the dress rehearsal; she is opening night.

It’s an exhausting, profoundly lonely feeling. It marinates your ego in a very specific kind of shame: *What is it about me that screams 'temporary'? Am I just palatable enough to pass the time with, but not remarkable enough to keep?*

Enter the psychology of the self-fulfilling prophecy. 

When you start viewing yourself as a pitstop, you subconsciously start acting like one. You absorb the narrative that you are a catalyst, not a destination. And that’s where the real damage happens.

Because I started believing I was cursed to be the "before" girl, I began dating like someone who expected to be left. I stopped asking for what I needed, terrified that pressing for commitment would speed up the inevitable expiration date. I picked men who were visibly emotionally unavailable—men like Ken, or men on the verge of moving across an ocean like Leo—because somewhere in my subconscious, *they fit the script*. If I picked a guy who was halfway out the door, I didn't have to face the terrifying prospect of a man who actually wanted to stay. 

I was building my own traps. By anticipating the end from day one, I kept one foot out the door. I withheld my own vulnerability under the guise of "protecting myself," which, ironically, created the very distance that drove these men into the arms of women who were brave enough to demand the whole pie, not just the crumbs.

We talk a lot about "Right Person, Wrong Time" in modern dating, but we rarely talk about the emotional toll of being the person who creates the "Right Time" for someone else. It makes you cynical. It turns dating from an adventure into an audition where you already know you won't get the lead role.

So, how do you close the portal? How do you stop being modern dating’s charity case?

You have to fire yourself from the job of Being the Educator. You have to stop raising grown men. You have to stop viewing a man’s potential as a personal project and start viewing his current behavior as his final offer. 

The next time I find myself wanting to gently guide a guy through his fear of intimacy, I’m pulling back. I am not a stepping stone, a layover, or a good luck charm. I am the destination. And if a guy needs a trial run to figure out how to treat a woman right, he can go buy a self-help book—I’m closing up shop.

counterfactuals.output:
I have a quietly neurotic habit, a kind of superstitious emotional insurance policy: I always run through the worst-case scenarios first. 

If I am on an airplane, I imagine the engine stalling, calculating the exact trajectory of our drop, under the absurd belief that if I envision the disaster, the universe will be stripped of its element of surprise and forced to keep us airborne. If I go for a medical checkup, I pre-grieve the worst possible diagnosis. And in love, I have spent years mentally writing the breakup speeches before the second date even arrives. I tell myself that if I picture the door closing, the strike of the lock won’t startle me when it happens. I think if I rehearse the heartbreak, I will be immune to the sting.

It is a exhausting way to live, this constant pre-disaster prep. But worse than the exhaustion is the ultimate uselessness of the ritual. Because no matter how vividly you map out the wreck, it still leaves you breathless when the metal twists.

Case in point: a Tuesday evening in late October. My phone buzzed on the nightstand, casting a harsh blue rectangle against the dim light of my bedroom. It was a text from a man I’ll call David, who had packed up his life two months prior to go on a "soul-searching sabbatical" through southern Europe. 

We hadn't ended things with a slam of a door, but rather a slow, wistful fade. He needed to "find his footing." He needed to wander the cobblestones of Portugal and Spain to figure out what he wanted from the second act of his life. I had spent weeks mentally preparing for him to fade out entirely. I had imagined him forgetting to text back, imagined him getting absorbed in work, imagined him deciding to move overseas permanently. I thought I had covered every dark alleyway of potential hurt.

Then the notification popped up. 

*I met someone,* it read. *In Lisbon. It’s strange, I wasn’t looking for anything, but she just completely turned my world upside down. I thought you should hear it from me.*

I stared at the screen, watching the little blue bubble hold its breath. I felt that familiar, hollow thrum in my chest—not just the shock of his news, but the bitter, ironic realization that my emotional pre-disaster prep had failed again. I had prepared for him to lose himself. I hadn't prepared for him to find himself with a woman he’d known for three weeks in a seaside hostel.

And then came the real tide, the heavier one: the sudden, crushing awareness of a pattern I thought I had broken. 

I sat on the edge of my bed and felt like a monument to interim love. I was, once again, the pitstop.

It was a role I had played with depressing consistency. There was Marcus, who spent two years in my apartment agonizing over his career, terrified of commitment, claiming he was too emotionally damaged from his past to ever step into marriage. Six months after we broke up, he was engaged to a woman he met at a pottery class, posting captions about "knowing from the moment he saw her." I had been the rehearsal; she was the opening night.

There was Julian, whom I spent months coaching through his anxieties, teaching him how to articulate his feelings, how to show up when things got uncomfortable, how to apologize with grace. He absorbed the lessons, packed his bags, and took those newly acquired emotional skill sets straight into a relationship with a colleague he married a year later. I was the rough draft; she got the polished final manuscript.

I was the cozy layover before the final destination. The transitional woman. The warm, supportive environment where men came to patch up their tires, fill their tanks, and learn how to drive, only to pull back out onto the highway and accelerate toward "the one."

It is a uniquely bittersweet feeling to realize you are good for people, but not *good enough to stay for*. There is a subtle cruelty in being the catalyst for someone else’s readiness. You provide the safety, the patience, the gentle mirror that allows them to fix their broken parts. You do the heavy lifting of the unglamorous work—the late-night conversations about their flaws, the encouragement through their doubts—and then someone else walks in to reap the harvest of the garden you helped water.

Sitting there with David’s text glowering in the dark, I felt a deep, reflective quiet settle over me. For years, I had blamed myself for these departures. I thought if I had just been a little prettier, a little funnier, a little less available, or a little more challenging, I would have been the destination instead of the pitstop. I thought my worst-case-scenario magic was failing because I wasn't imagining the pain hard enough.

But looking at the phone, I finally saw the flaw in my logic.

The superstition of pre-grieving wasn't protecting me; it was keeping me parked in the waiting room. By constantly preparing for men to leave, I was unconsciously accepting the role of the temporary. I was offering myself up as a sanctuary, a safe place for them to heal, while secretly waiting for the inevitable moment they realized they belonged somewhere else. I was acting like a layover, so they treated me like one.

David was in Lisbon, probably sitting at a sunlit cafe with a woman whose hand he held without overthinking, without fear, without the heavy burden of "searching." And I was here, in my bedroom, holding a phone that had delivered the exact tragedy I had spent weeks rehearsing.

It hurt. It hurt with the dull, familiar ache of an old scar caught in the cold. But beneath the sadness, a small, stubborn shift occurred. 

I opened the text thread. I didn't type out a bitter manifesto, nor did I play the part of the gracious, self-sacrificing martyr who tells him how happy I am for him. I just typed: *I'm glad you found what you were looking for.* 

Then, I deleted his number. 

I closed my eyes and stopped running the worst-case scenarios. I didn't picture the next guy leaving, or the next text message, or the next engagement announcement on social media. I let the future sit in the dark, un-rehearsed and unpredictable. 

I am tired of being the place where people get ready for their lives to begin. I am tired of being the mid-station, the pitstop, the dress rehearsal. The next time someone pulls into my life, they can either park the car for good, or they can keep driving. But I am finally done providing the tune-up.

# What makes men connect with the girl of their dreams after sparking with me?

If you’ve ever seen the 2007 romantic comedy *Good Luck Chuck*, you already know the premise: Dane Cook plays a guy who discovers that every woman he sleeps with finds her true soulmate immediately after breaking up with him. He becomes a literal lucky charm for everyone else’s happily-ever-after. 

I used to laugh at that movie. Now? I live it. 

I am the real-life, female version of "Good Luck Chuck." 

If we go on a few amazing dates, have undeniable chemistry, and share a late-night deep conversation where you open up about your childhood dreams... congratulations. You are roughly 3 to 6 months away from proposing to the woman you’re going to spend the rest of your life with. 

My dating history reads like a launchpad for long-term commitment:
* **Ex #1:** Dated for three months. We broke up; he met "Her" two weeks later. They are now married with a golden retriever. 
* **Ex #2:** Electric connection, amazing dates, but "he wasn't ready for a relationship." A month later, he made a girl he met at a coffee shop his official girlfriend. They just bought a house.
* **Ex #3:** The guy who "didn't believe in marriage." Guess who got engaged on a cliffside in Amalfi last summer? 

For a long time, I took this personally. Was I just a pit stop? Was I the romantic dress rehearsal? But after observing this pattern more times than I care to admit, I stopped sulking and started analyzing. 

I began to ask myself: *What is actually happening here? What makes men connect so deeply with the girl of their dreams right after sparking with me?*

Here is what I’ve realized about my strange, unofficial superpower.

---

### 1. I Flip the "Emotional Availability" Switch
A lot of men go through life on romantic autopilot. They date casually, keep their walls up, and avoid real vulnerability because it feels risky. 

When a man dates me, I don't do superficial. I ask real questions. I listen. I create a space where it is safe for them to drop the cool-guy persona and just be themselves. For many of these guys, sparking with me is the first time in years they’ve felt a genuine, intoxicating emotional connection. 

It wakes them up. It acts as an emotional defibrillator. 

Once that "feeling" switch is flipped back on, they can't flip it off. Even if we realize we aren't long-term compatible, the desire for deep connection has been reawakened in them. They go out into the world *actively looking* for love, often walking right into the arms of the girl they end up marrying. 

### 2. I Raise the Bar (And Provide the "Practice")
I have high standards. I don't accept low-effort text conversations, last-minute "u up?" invites, or half-hearted dates. If a guy wants to date me, he has to show up, plan thoughtful outings, and communicate.

In a way, I am a high-intensity training course for relationships. 

By the time things fizzle out between us, he has spent weeks or months learning how to be a better partner. He’s learned how to listen better, how to plan a proper date, and how to communicate his feelings. The next girl doesn't get the unpolished, low-effort version of him—she gets the upgraded, refined version that *I* helped shape. (You're welcome, ladies.)

### 3. The "Regret & Recovery" Effect
Sometimes, a man doesn't realize what he has until it’s gone. 

When things end between us—often because he freaked out over how fast things were moving or panicked about getting serious—a period of regret usually follows. He realizes that holding back cost him a great connection. 

That loss causes a sudden shift in perspective. The next time he meets a woman he feels a spark with, he thinks: *“I’m not making the same mistake twice. I’m not letting this one slip away.”* 

He locks her down immediately. My departure creates the urgency that makes him commit to the next person.

### 4. Extreme Clarity
Sparking with someone who is passionate, independent, and clear about who they are acts like a mirror. It forces a man to look at his life and ask: *What do I actually want?*

Sometimes, the spark between us highlights the exact puzzle piece that was missing in his life. Maybe he realizes he wants someone more low-key, or someone who shares a specific niche interest, or someone who fits a different vision of his future. Sparking with me gives him *clarity*. When he meets the girl of his dreams next, he recognizes her instantly because the contrast is so stark.

---

### The Catalyst's Dilemma

Being the "Good Luck Chuck" of the dating world is a strange space to occupy. On one hand, it’s frustrating to feel like the muse who inspires the masterpiece, only to be left out of the gallery. You start to wonder when it’s going to be *your* turn to be the destination, not just the stepping stone.

But on the other hand, it’s a weird point of pride. 

It means my energy is transformative. It means the time men spend with me makes them better, softer, more open, and more ready for love than I found them. I’m not leaving people broken; I’m leaving them ready. 

And if universe-level karma is real, I have to believe that sooner or later, a man is going to spark with *me*—and realize that he doesn't need to look any further for the girl of his dreams.

Until then, if you're a guy who wants to find his future wife... my schedule is open next Thursday.

### Always the Warm-Up Act: Am I Cursed to Prep Men for Their "Dream Girls"?

**By [Your Name]** | *October 14, 2007*

At 2:14 AM last night, the unmistakable, tinny double-buzz of my pink Motorola Razr woke me up. I flipped it open, illuminating my dark bedroom with that harsh blue glow, expecting a late-night “you awake?” from Julian. You know, Julian—my ex of three months who moved to London for a semester abroad, leaving us in that ambiguous, agonizing “let’s just see what happens” limbo.

Instead, I got a masterpiece of T9 text-speak efficiency: 

*“Hey. Hope ur good. Needed to tell u before u saw on FB. Met someone here. It’s diff. She’s the one. Ttyl.”*

I stared at the screen until the backlight dimmed. *She’s the one.* 

Naturally, I did what any emotionally stable girl in 2007 would do: I slammed the phone shut, blasted Kelly Clarkson’s “Since U Been Gone,” poured a glass of questionable Pinot Grigio, and logged onto AIM to change my away message to something aggressively passive-aggressive. (*“Some people change their minds like the weather... off to get a venti iced latte.”*)

But after the initial wave of humiliation washed over me, a terrifying realization settled in. This isn’t the first time this has happened. In fact, it’s a pattern. A sick, twisted, cosmic trend. 

Before Julian, there was Dave, who took the emotional intelligence I spent a year beating into him and immediately used it to woo a girl who wears low-rise True Religion jeans and works in PR. Before Dave, there was Mark, who swore he “wasn’t the marriage type” while we were dating, only to propose to a flight attendant six months after we split. 

I am, in the most painful, Dane Cook-esque sense of the phrase, a real-life *Good Luck Chuck*. I am the emotional boot camp. I am the starter girlfriend. Men enter my life disorganized, emotionally repressed, and wearing cargo shorts, and they exit as polished, self-actualized husbands-in-training for the very next girl who walks by.

Which leaves me huddled over my laptop at 3:00 AM, staring at my Facebook News Feed, asking the ultimate existential question: Is always being the precursor to a guy’s "dream girl" just astronomical bad luck, or is it a self-fulfilling prophecy?

#### Theory A: The Cosmic "Fixer-Upper" Curse

Let’s look at the bad luck theory first. Maybe some of us are just born with a sign on our foreheads that reads *“FREE EMOTIONAL LABOR: INQUIRE WITHIN.”* 

We’re the girls who listen to them cry about their dads. We’re the ones who teach them that washcloths need to be laundered and that a mattress doesn't belong directly on the floor. We do the heavy lifting. We take a rough draft of a man and do a rigorous, uncredited rewrite. 

By the time they break our hearts, they’re finally ready for prime time. But because the universe has a warped sense of humor, we don't get to enjoy the finished product. Instead, some girl named Chloe reaps the benefits of the communication skills *I* bled for. It feels like bad luck—like being the sacrificial lamb on the altar of male character development.

#### Theory B: The "Cool Girl" Prophecy

But then I took a sip of my wine and looked in the mirror. And that’s when the ugly truth started creeping in. What if it’s not the universe? What if it’s *me*?

Am I subverting my own happiness because I’m terrified of actually being seen? 

I play the "Cool Girl." I’m the girlfriend who doesn't demand the label, who says "let's just go with the flow," who acts totally fine with him going to Prague or London without a clear commitment because I don't want to seem "high maintenance." I act like a pit stop, so they treat me like one. 

When you position yourself as the warm-up act, you shouldn't be surprised when they save their best performance for the main event. 

By taking broken men and trying to "fix" them, I get a false sense of security. If I’m the caretaker, I’m in control. But broken men eventually heal, and when they do, they don't want to be reminded of the time when they were broken. They want a fresh start with a girl who expects them to be a finished product from Day One. 

#### Slamming the Razr Shut

Julian’s new girl is probably lovely. She probably wears cute berets and doesn't spend three hours analyzing T9 texts with her friends on AIM. Good for her. Honestly. 

But I’m officially retiring from the Girlfriend Rehabilitation Center. The next guy who comes into my life isn't getting a DIY project where I provide the tools. He’s going to have to show up fully assembled, or he can keep walking. 

I’m closing my Razr, deleting his number, and changing my Facebook status to Single. No away messages, no vague sub-tweets (or whatever we’re calling status updates this week). 

I'm nobody's practice run anymore. Next time, *I’m* the dream girl. 

***

*Ladies, have you ever felt like the "starter kit" for a guy's ultimate romance? How did you break the cycle? Sound off in the comments below!*
